Piper turns drawings, specifications, addenda, and company knowledge into trade-specific scopes, so your team can define what is included, clarify boundaries, and catch what still needs attention before bids go out. Build a trade scope on your project In short Piper builds trade-specific scopes from drawings, specifications, addenda, and company knowledge, using one evolving understanding of the project. It is not a spec writer or takeoff tool: it builds trade scope from the full project context. It is for general contractor preconstruction teams, especially estimators and preconstruction managers. Every requirement stays linked to its source in the project documents, and changes carry through the scopes they affect. The job today The scope is scattered across the project. Your scope sheet shouldn't be A complete trade scope rarely lives in one place. Requirements are spread across drawings, specifications, addenda, alternates, owner requirements, and the details experienced estimators know to look for. Before a package goes out, someone has to pull all of that together and decide what the trade is actually responsible for. Today Hours reading across drawings and specs. Old scope sheets copied from previous projects. Trade boundaries depend on who remembers to check them. Requirements buried in notes, details, and general conditions. With Piper Project requirements organized by trade. Each scope item linked back to its source. Trade boundaries and unclear responsibilities surfaced for review. Your company standards carried into every new scope. How scope generation works in Piper From scattered project requirements to a scope ready for review 01. Understand the project Bring the scope together from across the documents Piper reviews drawings, specifications, addenda, bid instructions, alternates, allowances, and other project requirements to build a structured picture of the work. 02. Organize by trade Turn project requirements into package-specific scope Requirements are organized around the trades and work packages that need to carry them, including items that appear across multiple documents or sit between traditional trade boundaries. 03. Challenge the scope Surface what is unclear, missing, or needs a decision Piper flags uncertain ownership, potential gaps and overlaps, relevant coordination requirements, and items that need estimator judgment before the scope is issued. 04. Build the scope sheet Put the work into your company's format Generate a trade-specific scope with inclusions, applicable requirements, alternates, allowances, coordination items, and source references, ready for your team to review before solicitation. More than drawing notes Build the scope behind the bid package Trade responsibilities Included work Trade ownership Furnished-by / installed-by boundaries Potential gaps and overlaps Project requirements Drawings Specifications Addenda Owner requirements Alternates and allowances Coordination scope Blocking and backing Cutting and patching Sleeves and penetrations Firestopping Controls and connections Testing and commissioning Project conditions Phasing Site logistics Temporary protection Hoisting Submittals and closeout Schedule requirements Every requirement stays connected to the project source behind it Outcomes Send better scope out before the bids come back Start from the project, not the last job Use the current drawings, specifications, addenda, and requirements as the basis of the scope instead of relying on someone to remember what should be copied from an old package. Catch the awkward scope between trades The expensive misses are often not the obvious systems. They are the interfaces: who provides blocking, firestopping, controls integration, testing, patching, temporary protection, or another requirement sitting between packages. Spend estimator time on judgment Piper does the extraction and organization so experienced people can spend more time deciding trade boundaries, challenging unclear requirements, and identifying what the documents may not fully resolve. Give every bidder the same basis A clearer scope gives subcontractors a more consistent definition of what to price, making the bids that come back easier to compare and level. Define the work before you ask someone to price it Build a real trade scope with Piper Bring drawings and specifications from a current or recent project. Piper compares subcontractor bids against the project scope, not just against each other, so you can see what is included, what is missing, and what each bid really costs before you make the call. Level a trade package on your project In short Piper evaluates subcontractor bids against the required project scope, not only against each other. It is not simple bid tabulation or side-by-side quote comparison: it evaluates bids against the actual required scope. It is for general contractor preconstruction teams, especially estimators and preconstruction managers. Exclusions, gaps, and the leveled number stay grounded in source documents, and those findings carry into the estimate they affect. The job today The low bid is only low if it carries the work Subcontractor proposals rarely arrive apples to apples. One includes what another excludes. One acknowledges the latest addendum. Another leaves a scope item silent. Before you can compare the numbers, you have to understand what is actually behind them. Today Different quote formats. Scope buried across proposals and attachments. Hours checking exclusions, qualifications, and missing items. Manual plugs just to understand the comparable number. With Piper Every bid structured in one comparable view. Each proposal checked against the intended scope. Gaps, exclusions, and qualifications surfaced with their sources. Raw bid and leveled position visible before you choose a carry. How bid leveling works in Piper From subcontractor proposals to a carry you can defend 01. Bring the package together Quotes, scope, and project requirements in one context Upload subcontractor proposals as they arrive alongside the trade scope and relevant project information. Piper reads PDFs, spreadsheets, and attachments without requiring every bidder to follow the same format. 02. Understand every bid See what each subcontractor actually priced Piper extracts base bid, inclusions, exclusions, qualifications, alternates, allowances, unit prices, addenda acknowledgments, and other terms that affect the comparison. 03. Level scope and cost Compare each proposal against the work you need covered Piper aligns the bids to the same scope, surfaces missing or overlapping work, and shows where addbacks, deductions, or clarification may be needed to make the numbers comparable. 04. Make the carry decision See the number and what is behind it Review raw bids, leveling adjustments, open clarifications, and source-backed scope differences in one place. Piper directs attention to what needs judgment; your team decides the number to carry. Piper puts scope differences beside price so the raw low bid does not hide an expensive gap. Catch exposure before carry See exclusions, qualifications, missing addenda, and uncovered scope while there is still time to clarify or adjust, not after the number is already in the estimate. Piper reviews your estimate against the project behind it: drawings, specifications, addenda, scopes, subcontractor bids, and company checks, so your team can see what may be missing, duplicated, stale, or unresolved before you commit. Review an estimate on your project In short Piper reviews the estimate against the project behind it: drawings, specifications, addenda, scopes, and bids. It is not a static checklist or a replacement for estimator judgment: it is a project-aware second check before submission. It is for general contractor preconstruction teams, especially estimators and preconstruction managers. Missing scope, duplicated cost, and unresolved risk stay grounded in source documents so senior review can focus on what still needs judgment. The job today A finished estimate can still hide unfinished decisions The estimate can balance and every line can have a number while important scope is still missing, an old assumption is still being carried, or the same requirement is priced twice. Before submission, someone has to challenge the estimate against everything the team knows about the project. Today Senior estimators review thousands of lines under deadline pressure. Scope, bids, addenda, and estimate decisions live in different places. Late changes are easy to miss. Review depends on what each person remembers to check. With Piper The estimate checked against the current project context. Missing and duplicated scope surfaced for review. Stale or unsupported carry decisions called out. Senior attention directed to the issues that actually need judgment. How Final Bid Review works in Piper From a finished estimate to a submission your team has challenged 01. Connect the estimate Bring the number together with the project behind it Piper reviews your estimate alongside drawings, specifications, addenda, trade scopes, subcontractor bids, and other relevant project information instead of treating the estimate as a standalone spreadsheet. 02. Trace what you're carrying Understand what sits behind the estimate Piper connects estimate lines to the scope, pricing source, subcontractor coverage, allowances, plugs, and project requirements that support them. 03. Challenge the estimate Look for what does not line up Piper cross-checks the current estimate for missing scope, duplicated cost, uncovered requirements, stale information, inconsistent assumptions, and other conditions that deserve another look. 04. Focus the final review Put senior judgment where it matters most Instead of asking a reviewer to reperform the entire estimate, Piper surfaces and prioritizes the open issues, with the evidence behind each one. Your team decides what to change, accept, qualify, or carry. Review the latest project, not yesterday's version Late addenda, revised quotes, scope changes, and new clarifications can invalidate work that was already considered finished. Piper helps surface where those changes may affect the current estimate.
